title: Recognise agri/ecotourism within the strategic environment

lessons.title: The strategic environment of agri/ecotourism
lessons.html:
Thinking strategically

A farm tourism venture does not operate in isolation. Its success depends on trends and forces in the wider tourism industry, the economy, government policy, the environment and the local community. Recognising these forces helps managers spot opportunities, avoid threats and position the venture.

The tourism industry context

Tourism is an important sector in South Africa's economy and a significant employer, supported by national tourism policy and destination marketing. Rural and nature-based tourism, including wine routes, game farms, hiking and cycling trails, farm stays and food experiences, forms part of the national tourism offering. Domestic tourism (South Africans travelling locally) and international tourism behave differently: domestic visitors are more price-sensitive and travel more on weekends and school holidays; international visitors are affected by exchange rates, flight access and global events.

PESTEL analysis

FactorExamples for farm tourism
PoliticalTourism policy, visa rules, land reform, local government support for rural development
EconomicExchange rate, fuel prices, consumer spending, interest rates
SocialGrowing interest in authentic, outdoor, food and wellness experiences; safety perceptions
TechnologicalOnline booking platforms, social media marketing, reviews, connectivity in rural areas
EnvironmentalDrought, fire, climate change, biodiversity value, water availability for guests
LegalAccommodation grading, zoning and land use rights, health and safety, liquor and food licences, labour law

Stakeholders

  • Tourists and tour operators
  • Local tourism organisations and route associations
  • Provincial and national tourism bodies
  • Conservation authorities and conservancies
  • Local communities and neighbouring farmers
  • Municipalities, for roads, services and land use
  • Financing and development agencies

Building relationships with these stakeholders opens access to marketing, funding and support.

lessons.title: Positioning a farm tourism venture strategically
lessons.html:
SWOT for the venture

Combine the external PESTEL picture with an internal assessment of the farm's strengths and weaknesses. Example for a fruit farm near a national route:

  • Strengths: scenic setting, working orchards, historic farmhouse, skilled staff.
  • Weaknesses: gravel access road, limited accommodation, no tourism experience.
  • Opportunities: growing weekend market from nearby cities, wine and food routes, school education trips.
  • Threats: competing venues, drought affecting landscape appeal, economic downturn.

Choosing a strategic position

  • Target markets: families, school groups, international nature tourists, corporate groups, events.
  • Unique selling points: what makes the farm different, such as a heritage story, rare birds, hands-on harvest, farm-to-table meals.
  • Product mix: day visits, accommodation, food, activities, retail of farm products.
  • Pricing: aligned to market, value delivered and competitors.
  • Partnerships: join route associations, collaborate with neighbours to create multi-day itineraries.

Integration with farming

Tourism must complement, not undermine, the farming enterprise. Consider biosecurity (visitors near livestock can introduce disease; controlled access and footbaths may be needed), chemical spray schedules and re-entry periods, harvest peaks and staff workload, and insurance and liability.

Sustainability and responsible tourism

Responsible tourism principles call for minimising negative environmental, social and economic impacts, generating local benefits, involving local people, contributing to conservation and respecting culture. Practically: save water and energy, manage waste, employ and train local people, buy locally, and protect natural areas. These practices increasingly attract visitors and can support certification or awards.

Risk management

  • Safety of visitors: risk assessments, signage, trained staff, first aid, emergency plans.
  • Legal compliance: licences, zoning, health regulations.
  • Financial risk: phased development, test the market before large investments.

Monitoring

Track visitor numbers, revenue per visitor, occupancy, reviews and repeat visits. Watch external trends and adapt.

Key points

  • Farm tourism operates within industry, economic, policy and environmental forces.
  • Use PESTEL and SWOT to analyse the strategic environment.
  • Identify target markets, unique selling points and partnerships.
  • Integrate tourism with farming, managing biosecurity and chemical safety.
  • Apply responsible tourism principles and monitor performance.
